title: Composition (Rachana)
tagline: One composition from a changing set of subjects and stimuli: plan it, shape it and write it in clean Hindi.

sourceNote.boardprep: All notes, model openings, practice passages, vocabulary, questions and answers on this page are original BoardPrep material written against the CISCE ICSE Examination Year 2028 second-language syllabus registered for this subject. The names, addresses and institutions used in the models are fictional, and the practice passage is BoardPrep’s own writing rather than any prescribed or previously used text.

overview.intro: The syllabus records the composition task in deliberately open terms: you write one composition, the subjects vary, and they may arrive as prompts or stimuli — pictures or objects — with the writing called on to explain, give directions, describe or narrate. Openness is not vagueness; it means the skill being examined is the writing itself, because no topic can be memorised in advance. What can be prepared is everything around the topic: how to read a stimulus and decide what it is asking for, how to turn a first impression into a paragraph plan, how to hold one central point across a page of continuous Hindi, and how to check the finished work for the faults that cost marks even when the ideas are good. This chapter works through those four modes, the planning that precedes every sentence, and the discipline that keeps tense, paragraphing and spelling under control.

learningOutcomes: Restate what the syllabus statement records about the composition task and its four modes.
Turn a picture or object prompt into a plan with one central point and an ordered list of paragraphs.
Structure a composition into an introduction, a developed body and a conclusion that returns to the point.
Keep tense, agreement and spelling under control across a page of continuous Hindi writing.
Apply a checking routine that catches structural and grammatical faults before the work is submitted.

learn.title: What the syllabus actually asks for

blocks.text: The syllabus is deliberately open about this task: you write one composition, the subjects vary, and they may arrive as prompts or stimuli — pictures or objects — with the writing called on to explain, give directions, describe or narrate. Openness in the statement is a design, not an oversight: because the topic cannot be predicted, what is examined is the writing itself — the selection of material, the ordering of it into paragraphs, and the correctness of the Hindi it is expressed in. Whatever the subject, the same four movements apply: decide which mode the prompt wants, gather the points your paragraphs will develop, hold one central point across the page, and express it in sentences whose tense and grammar stay consistent from the first line to the last.

blocks.caption: The four modes the syllabus names, and how each treats the same material
rows: Make a subject or situation clear: what it means and why it happens
explain, the reason for, what it means
Give the steps of a process in the order they must be carried out
how to, the steps of, first, then, finally
Present a place, scene, event or person in developed, observed detail
describe, the scene of, what you see
Tell an event as a connected story, normally in the past tense

learn.title: Reading the prompt before writing a word

items: Underline the keywords of the prompt — the subject, the demanded mode and any limit it states — so that your eyes return to them rather than to your imagination.
Decide the mode explicitly: explanation, directions, description or narration. Every later choice, from tense to paragraph shape, follows from this one decision.
Fix the person and the tense before the first sentence, and keep them: a narration normally lives in the past, an explanation in an explanatory present.
List four or six points in the order you will develop them — this list is the composition in skeleton form and takes only a minute.
Decide your opening sentence and your closing thought while planning, so that the page begins and ends where you intended rather than wherever you stopped.

blocks.text: This reading takes five minutes and saves much more, because writing without it produces the commonest failure in long answers: a first paragraph that wanders and a middle with no direction. When the mode is decided late, the opening has to be crossed out and rewritten; when the point list is missing, each paragraph invents its own purpose and the page accumulates rather than develops. The prompt is short, but it contains everything the task depends on — subject, mode and limits — and candidates who lose marks here rarely lose them in grammar. Read it twice: once for what it says, once for what it demands, and begin only when both readings agree.

learn.title: From point list to paragraph plan

blocks.text: A composition holds together when every paragraph advances one central point — the single sentence about what this composition is saying. The introduction states that point in two or three sentences, the body develops it one aspect per paragraph, and the conclusion returns to it rather than opening something new. Paragraphing is how this becomes visible to the reader: a paragraph takes one idea, develops it with a detail or an example, and hands over to the next through a connecting word, so that the movement of thought can be seen on the page. Without paragraphs the points run together and the reader must do the sorting the writer should have done; without a central point the paragraphs may each be correct while the page as a whole says nothing at all.

items: Introduction: two or three sentences that name the subject and indicate the central point — nothing that the body will have to repeat.
Body: one point per paragraph, each developed with a detail, an example or a reason, in the order fixed during planning.
Links: connecting words between paragraphs — fir, isliye, lekin, ant men — so the reader is carried rather than dropped.
Conclusion: two sentences that return to the central point and close it, not a new idea introduced at the last moment.

items.text: पिछले रविवार हम सब गए। सब कुछ अच्छा था।
items.note: A flat opening: it starts at random and gives the reader nothing to hold — who went, where, and why it matters are all missing.

items.text: पिछले रविवार की पार्क की सैर ने मुझे बताया कि शहर के बीच भी प्रकृति साँस ले रही है।
items.note: An opening with a central point: the occasion and the claim arrive together, so every paragraph that follows has a direction to serve.

blocks.text: Development is the difference between listing and writing. A point earns its paragraph when it is given a detail, an example or a reason that explains why the point is true — one concrete image, one remembered instance, one consequence. Description draws on what the senses could report; narration moves through causes and effects in time; explanation follows a reason to its conclusion; directions keep the steps in an order that would actually work. Drift begins when a paragraph has no such obligation: it repeats the introduction in new words, or follows an interesting tangent that the central point never asked for. Read each finished paragraph and ask what it adds that the previous one did not — if the honest answer is nothing, the paragraph is padding and should be cut or merged.

items.meaning: The one sentence your whole composition serves; every paragraph must advance it in some way.
The closing paragraph that returns to the central idea instead of introducing a new subject.
Words such as fir, isliye, lekin and ant men that carry the reader between sentences and paragraphs.
The order in which points appear — narration and directions depend on it completely.
Selecting the word you actually mean, especially between near-synonyms of different register.

learn.title: Keeping the Hindi correct under time

blocks.text: Continuous writing is where grammar quietly fails, because attention is on content and the sentences are being produced at speed. The three faults that occur most often are tense shifts, disagreement between a verb and its subject, and spelling slips in high-frequency words. Tense is the one to settle first: a narration that begins in the past and slips into the present tells the reader that the sequence is confused, even when every sentence is individually correct. Agreement follows the subject in gender and number, and in Hindi it reaches the adjective and the participle as well. Both faults are cheap to repair — the checking pass at the end reads only the verbs, then only the subjects — but they must be looked for deliberately, because the writer who is still thinking about content will not notice them while writing.

items: Choose one tense for the narrative thread and hold it; a genuine shift of time may change it, but not a change of mood.
Make every finite verb agree with its subject in gender and number, including the adjectives and participles that lean on it.
Check the indeclinables and the commonly confused pairs — words that look alike but carry different registers.
Do not switch scripts or insert English words casually; borrow only the word your Hindi genuinely lacks, and use it consistently.
Read once for spelling of the words you use most — the same dozen words recur in every composition, and their spelling is worth a minute.

learn.title: The final check, and how to practise

items: Re-read the prompt first: is the subject answered, and the mode that was asked for actually used?
Count paragraphs: introduction, at least two developed body paragraphs, conclusion — and confirm each advances the central point.
Read only the verbs: any tense shift inside the narrative thread is now visible and cheap to fix.
Scan agreement: subject and verb, adjective and noun, in every sentence that carries a plural subject.
Check the ending: does the last paragraph return to the central point, or has a new idea wandered in?
Look once at spelling in the first and last sentences, which are read most carefully and remembered longest.

blocks.text: Practice turns this list into habit. Choose a past paper stimulus or a picture, give yourself a fixed limit you have chosen and keep to it, and write the whole composition without stopping — fluency comes from unbroken attempts, and stopping to perfect each sentence trains the wrong skill. Then spend the last minutes of the limit on exactly the two readings above: one for structure, one for verbs. Keep a list of your own recurring faults — a page is enough — and before the next attempt read only that list. Improvement in this task is rarely about new vocabulary; it is about the same faults not recurring, and a writer who knows their own three most frequent errors will find that fixing them lifts the whole page.

figures.caption: Figure: five moves from prompt to page
figures.description: A left-to-right flow of five boxed stages: the prompt with its keywords underlined; the mode decided from the four the syllabus names; a list of four to six points in order; a paragraph plan mapping each point to a paragraph with the introduction and conclusion marked; and a final check arrow returning over the whole plan. The mode box is drawn with a double border because every later stage depends on it.

figures.caption: Figure: the shape of a finished composition
figures.description: A stacked diagram of a completed page: a narrow introduction block at the top labelled with the central point, two or more body blocks of decreasing width beneath it each marked with one point and its detail, connecting arrows down the left margin showing the links between paragraphs, and a narrow conclusion block at the foot returning to the same central point — shown by a curved arrow back to the top block.

keyPoints: The syllabus records one composition on a varying subject, possibly presented as a picture or an object as a stimulus.
The four modes named are explanation, directions, description and narration — decide which one the prompt demands before writing.
Fix the central point in one sentence during planning; every paragraph must advance it.
Paragraphs are the visible form of structure: one developed idea per paragraph, linked by connecting words.
The introduction names the subject and point in two or three sentences; the conclusion returns to them and adds nothing new.
Tense, agreement and spelling fail under speed, so they are repaired in a deliberate checking pass, not while writing.
Description observes, narration sequences, explanation reasons, directions order — the mode decides the treatment.
Practice works with a self-set time limit and a personal fault list, because the same recurring faults are what suppress a page.
No composition subject is prescribed or repeated in advance; the writing skill is the only thing that transfers.
examFocus: Open by naming the subject and the central point together; the first two sentences set the direction of everything after them.
Identify the mode in the first paragraph of your plan — a description written where an explanation was asked reads as irrelevant.
Develop each point with one detail or example; a page of assertions without development is a list, not a composition.
Hold one tense through each narrative thread and re-read only the verbs before submitting.
Finish with a conclusion that returns to the central point — ending mid-discussion loses the closing impression of the whole.
Practise under a fixed self-set limit with a picture or object prompt, then audit your own recurring faults by name.

questions.prompt: According to the syllabus statement recorded for this subject, how many compositions does a candidate write?
options: One composition, on a subject that may vary
Two compositions, one formal and one informal
One composition for each prescribed book
questions.answer: One composition, on a subject that may vary
questions.explanation: The statement records a single composition whose subjects vary, so the skill being practised is the writing itself rather than the memorising of topics. The other options describe tasks this paper does not set.
questions.commonMistake: Preparing for two compositions because the letter task also appears in the same section — the letter is a separate task.

questions.prompt: Which of these can present a composition subject, as the syllabus statement records it?
options: A picture or an object used as a stimulus
A letter received from a friend
An unseen passage of about 250 words
questions.answer: A picture or an object used as a stimulus
questions.explanation: The statement says subjects may use prompts or stimuli such as pictures or objects. The other options belong to other tasks of the course: the prescribed texts, the letter and the comprehension passage.
questions.commonMistake: Treating the stimulus as decoration rather than as the subject — the picture is what the composition must grow from.

questions.prompt: The syllabus lists four modes the composition may call for. Which is NOT one of them?
options: Translation of a passage from English
questions.answer: Translation of a passage from English
questions.explanation: The four modes recorded are explanation, directions, description and narration. Translation is a separate language exercise, so a candidate who treats the composition as translation has misread the task entirely.
questions.commonMistake: Remembering three of the four and inventing a substitute — description is the mode most often left out of the list.

questions.prompt: What is the first job of a composition’s opening paragraph?
options: Name the subject and indicate the central point
List every point that the body will cover
State the conclusion to save time later
Copy the prompt word for word
questions.answer: Name the subject and indicate the central point
questions.explanation: An opening earns its place by fixing direction: within two or three sentences the reader should know what the composition is about and where it is going. The point list belongs in the plan, the conclusion at the end, and copying is not writing at all.
questions.commonMistake: Spending the opening on background scenery when the subject and point could have been named in the same sentences.

questions.prompt: Complete: each paragraph of a composition carries one ________ , and the composition ends with a ________ that returns to the central point.
questions.explanation: Paragraph discipline means one developed idea per paragraph so the reader can follow the movement, and the concluding paragraph closes the circle by returning to the central point instead of introducing a new subject.
questions.commonMistake: Starting a new paragraph for every sentence, which breaks the development of each point into fragments.

questions.prompt: State the four modes the syllabus names for the composition task, with one line on each.
questions.answer: Explanation — make a subject or situation clear by showing what it means or why it happens. Directions — give the steps of a process in the order they must be carried out. Description — present a place, scene, event or person in developed detail. Narration — tell an event as a connected story, normally in the past tense.
questions.explanation: The four names come straight from the syllabus statement registered for this subject, and the one-line gloss shows you can do more than repeat them: each mode implies a different treatment of the same material.
questions.commonMistake: Listing the four without the glosses, which shows recall but not that you can choose between the modes.

questions.prompt: What should you do first when a picture or an object is given as the prompt?
questions.answer: Look at the stimulus carefully before writing anything: identify what it actually shows, pick out the details that matter, decide which of the four modes the prompt is asking for, and only then list the four or five points your paragraphs will develop. The picture supplies the material; your reading of it decides the treatment.
questions.explanation: The first minutes decide the whole composition, because a picture can be read in several ways and each reading suggests a different mode. Deciding late means rewriting, so the reading comes before the plan and the plan before the first sentence.
questions.commonMistake: Describing every object visible in the picture instead of choosing the detail that serves one central point.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would plan and write a composition on a picture prompt, from the first reading to the final check.
questions.answer: First reading: take in the whole picture, then its details, and decide what it is about — a scene, an occasion, a contrast, a warning. Choose the mode that fits: describe what is visible, explain what it suggests, narrate what it could lead to, or give directions for acting on it. Note four or five points in the order you will develop them, fix the central point in one sentence, and decide the opening. Write the introduction in two or three sentences that name the subject and the central point, then develop one point per paragraph with a detail or example in each, using connectors so the reader can follow the movement. Keep the tense consistent — narration normally stays in the past — and prefer words you are sure of to impressive words you do not control. Close with a paragraph that returns to the central point. Finally, reread once for paragraphing, once for tense shifts and agreement, and once for the spelling of your common words, checking that every paragraph still serves the point set in the introduction.
questions.explanation: The method moves in a fixed order — read, choose the mode, list, plan, write, check — because each stage depends on the one before it. Content comes from the developed points and form from paragraphing and consistency, so the answer must show both stages explicitly.
questions.commonMistake: Beginning to write before deciding the mode, which produces an opening that describes when the task asked for explanation.

questions.prompt: Explain how paragraphing and a central point hold a long composition together, and what happens when either is missing.
questions.answer: The central point is the one sentence the whole composition serves, and every paragraph must advance it in some way. Paragraphing makes that advancement visible: each paragraph takes one idea, develops it with detail or example, and hands over to the next through a connector, so the movement of thought can be seen on the page. When the central point is missing the composition drifts — each paragraph may be correct on its own while the page as a whole says nothing, because no sentence has decided what the page is for. When paragraphing is missing, the points run together in one block and the reader must do the sorting the writer should have done. The two faults compound: an unplanned page with no centre is usually both shapeless and long. The cure belongs at the planning stage — fix the point, list the paragraphs, and check each finished paragraph against the point as you write.
questions.explanation: A strong answer explains the relationship instead of describing the two features separately: the point gives direction and paragraphing makes direction visible. The consequences must be concrete — drift and block — because that is what demonstrates understanding rather than recall.
questions.commonMistake: Describing paragraphing as merely visual, about neatness on the page, rather than as the structure of thought.

questions.prompt: A classmate writes a whole composition as one block and changes tense twice in the middle of a narration. Comment on both faults and show how to correct them.
questions.answer: The first fault is structural: one block means no paragraphing, so the reader cannot see where a point begins or ends, and the developed ideas inside the block are hidden behind a wall of text. The correction starts with the plan itself — break the point list into paragraphs, give each one idea with its detail, and start the next paragraph on a new line with a connector. The second fault is grammatical: a narration that begins in the past and slips into the present makes the sequence jump, so the verb forms no longer belong to the same timeline even when each sentence is individually correct. The correction is to fix the tense at the start — past for a narrated incident — and then to read only the verbs, so that every finite verb in the narrative thread sits in the same tense unless a genuine shift of time requires otherwise. Both faults share one cause: writing without a plan and without a checking pass. The practical fix is therefore a method, not two separate corrections — reserve the last minutes for two readings, one for structure and one for verbs.
questions.explanation: The comment must diagnose rather than disapprove: for each fault, give what it does to the reader and what change removes it. Ending with a single cause turns two complaints into one method, which is what lifts an analytical answer above a list of faults.
questions.commonMistake: Naming the faults without corrections, or treating the tense shifts as individual word errors rather than as one missing decision.
